Step 5 · Different Wiring

High-pass, band-pass, resonance: one mathematics, three appetites

Same R and C — just take the output across the resistor instead, and the low-pass becomes a high-pass on the spot: |H(jω)| = ωτ/√(1+(ωτ)²). Low frequencies are blocked, highs pass, and the −3 dB point sits at the same ωc = 1/τ. Drag τ and watch the cutoff run; compare with step 2’s low-pass Bode plot — the two are mirror images.

RC high-pass τ (ωc = 1/τ) 1.00 s（ωc = 1.00）

τ = 1.00 s · ωc = 1.00 rad/s · at ωc, |H| = 0.7071 and φ = +45.0° (the high-pass leads where the low-pass lags — same magnitude, opposite sign) · at ω = 0.1ωc, |H| = 0.0995 (lows cut to about a tenth)

One more step: put a low-pass and a high-pass back to back so only a middle band of frequencies passes — a band-pass. The standard second-order band-pass H(jω) = 1 / (1 + jQ(ω/ω₀ − ω₀/ω)) peaks at ω₀ with height 1, and the quality factor Q sets how fat the peak is — larger Q, sharper peak. One readout below is a live audit: the half-power bandwidth Δω measured off the curve (the distance between the two points where |H| falls to 1/√2 of the peak) must satisfy Q = ω₀/Δω — whether the measured number matches the slider is for the digits to say. This is a normalized band-pass output. A spring’s displacement/force response has a different numerator, so its peak location and height cannot be copied from this curve. Compare damping, displacement peaks and poles in the atlas →

Band-pass peak f₀ 100 Hz
Quality factor Q 5.00

f₀ = 100 Hz · Q set = 5.00 · measured half-power points f₁ = 90.5 Hz, f₂ = 110.5 Hz, Δf = 20.0 Hz · Q recovered from the measurement, f₀/Δf = 5.00 (audited against the setting)

Tuning a radio is band-pass work: the peak aims at the station, and Q decides whether the neighboring station bleeds in. Too small a Q and two stations mush together; too large and the peak is so sharp it shaves the station’s own high frequencies. Even pickiness has to be portioned right.

Step 4 · Drag the poles

A system’s character is written in its pole positions

Now a second-order system H(s) = 1/(s² + 2ζω0s + ω0²). Its pair of poles can be dragged around the s-plane: above the real axis they form a conjugate pair (the system rings as it decays); drag them back onto the real axis and the poles turn real — they can sit on top of each other (critical damping) or be pulled apart into two separate real poles (overdamped). On the right, the impulse response h(t) redraws in real time (closed form, not a numerical simulation) together with its ±envelope: the real part σp of the poles is the decay rate — the farther left of the axis, the harder the envelope eσpt squeezes it down. Drag them into the right half-plane and watch the envelope open upward instead: the response bursts the frame.

Stable ringing decay
Critically damped
Overdamped
Sustained oscillation
Blow-up
envelope probe time t 1.0

poles: −0.80 ± j2.40 · ζ = 0.316 · ω₀ = 2.530 · state: stable — the response decays to zero · envelope at t = 1.0: ±E = 0.187 (definition of E in the note under the figure)

Conventions: underdamped, h(t) = eσpt·sin(ωdt)/ωd with envelope E(t) = eσpt/ωd; critically damped, h(t) = t·ept and the curve is its own envelope; overdamped with real poles p1, p2, h(t) = (ep1t − ep2t)/(p1 − p2) and the envelope is the sum of the absolute components, (ep1t + ep2t)/|p1 − p2|. Everything is closed form; every point can be recomputed by hand.

One more word on the “—” in the readout: when the two real poles have opposite signs, ω₀ = √(p₁p₂) is imaginary and ζ is undefined — the “—” is the honest answer, not a missing computation; a pole sitting exactly at the origin gives ω₀ = 0 and is likewise undefined. When you see “—”, read the pole positions and the verdict instead: any pole in the right half-plane means the system is unstable.

Everything the PID controller does on the control page is one long fight to push the closed-loop poles into the left half-plane: the deeper they go, the steadier the cart and the faster it settles — go push them yourself over there →

Feedback & Control →

Get the feel of it: park the poles just left of the axis (σp ≈ −0.1) and watch the tail ring on and on; then yank them to σp = −2.5 and the tail is cut off at once. The smaller ζ is, the floatier the ringing; at ζ ≥ 1 it cannot ring at all — click through the five presets; it teaches faster than definitions.
